newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh's parents plead for his life.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh's parents plead for his life.

text.p: The parents of convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh pleaded with the jury to spare his life before the defence rested its case on Wednesday in the sentencing phase of his trial.
"He is not the monster he has been portrayed as," said his mother Mildred Frazer, reading tearfully from a statement she had prepared in advance.
The mood in the courtroom was even more sombre than usual. McVeigh smiled weakly at his mother as she entered the room and could be seen wiping away tears as she wept.
McVeigh's parents were the last witnesses to testify on his behalf during the sentencing phase, and the defence rested its case after William McVeigh's testimony.
Closing arguments were scheduled for Thursday morning, and the jury was expected to begin deliberating soon after.
McVeigh, a former soldier, was convicted on June 2 of the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Oklahoma City federal office building, an attack that killed 168 people and injured more than 500 others.
During this phase of the trial, the jury was to decide whether McVeigh should be executed or spend his life in prison.
Asked outside the courtroom what he would say in his closing argument, chief defence attorney Stephen Jones said: "We're going to ask them to spare his life."

McVeigh's mother wrote that she could not begin to imagine the pain and suffering of the bombing victims and that she could understand their anger, adding, "I cannot believe to this day he could have caused this devastation."
"Yes, I am pleading for my son's life," she said. "He is a human being just as we all are."
Frazer was briefly committed involuntarily earlier this year to a hospital for what authorities called "psychotic behaviour."
McVeigh's father followed his ex-wife on the witness stand and narrrated a 10-minute videotape the defence made about his son's childhood. The couple divorced in 1986.

The elder McVeigh betrayed no emotion and did not look toward his son. McVeigh's sister Jennifer, who testified with immunity against him during the guilt or innocence phase of his trial, also sat in the courtroom and did not react visibly to her parent's testimony.

The videotape narrated by William McVeigh included home movies made by McVeigh's grandfather at their home in western New York. It showed childhood activities such as McVeigh, whom he called "Timmy," jumping off a diving board and later graduating from high school.
McVeigh's father concluded his testimony by displaying a photo of him with his arm around his son in the early 1990's. "It's a happy Tim," he said. "It's a Tim I remember most of my life."
"Do you love the Tim McVeigh in this picture?" defence attorney Richard Burr said.
"Yes," he replied.
"Do you love the Tim McVeigh in the courtroom?" Burr asked.
"Yes," he said.
"Do you want him to stay alive?" Burr asked.
"Yes, I do," McVeigh said.
In its rebuttal, prosecutor Larry Mackey read a letter written by McVeigh to a newspaper in 1992.
"Is a civil war imminent? Do we have to shed blood to reform the current system? I hope it doesn't come to that. But it might," the letter read.
The judge sent the jury home and ordered them to return on Thursday at 8:30 a.m. (1430 GMT)
"You've now heard all you're going to hear with respect to the evidence and information," he told them.
